title: Combining AR and MA
objectives: Fit an ARMA model and choose its orders by AIC
Judge the chosen model by its residuals and out-of-sample error

screens.title: Neither rule fits
screens.prose: A new seeded series of 500 days, `make_arma([0.7], [0.4], 500, 33)`. Top: its ACF. Bottom: its PACF. The band is $\pm 0.0877$ in both.
screens.question: Which cut-off rule from lessons 8 and 9 names the model?

options.text: Neither: the ACF and the PACF both tail off
MA(1): the biggest ACF bar is at lag 1
options.why: An MA(1) ACF drops into the band after lag 1. Here lag 2 is 0.605 and lag 6 is still 0.1841.

options.text: AR(1): the biggest PACF bar is at lag 1
options.why: An AR(1) PACF drops into the band after lag 1. Here lags 2 and 3 are −0.3216 and 0.1173, outside it.

hints.text: A cut-off means the bars fall into the band and stay there.
Look at lags 2 and 3 in each panel.
The ACF is still outside the band at lag 8; the PACF is outside at lags 2 and 3.

feedback.correct: Correct. Both decay, so neither rule gives the order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether either panel falls into the band after one lag and stays.

explain.text: The ACF decays slowly (0.8367, 0.605, 0.432, ...) and the PACF decays with alternating sign (0.8384, −0.3216, 0.1173). An AR alone would cut the PACF; an MA alone would cut the ACF. This series has both an AR part and an MA part.

screens.title: Two dials
screens.prose: The green bars are the theoretical ACF of $x_t = \phi x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t + \theta\varepsilon_{t-1}$. With $\theta = 0$ it is an AR(1); with $\phi = 0$ an MA(1). Move both sliders until the green bars match the blue.

let.r1: (1 + phi * theta) * (phi + theta) / (1 + 2 * phi * theta + theta * theta)

screens.question: Which setting matches the sample best?

options.why: You matched lag 1 with an AR(1). Then lag 2 is $0.84^2 \approx 0.70$, above the sample 0.605, and the tail stays too high.
An MA(1) cannot pass 0.5 at lag 1, and it has nothing at lag 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try matching lag 1 and lag 2 together.

explain.text: At $\phi = 0.7$, $\theta = 0.4$ the theory gives 0.819 at lag 1, then each lag is 0.7 times the one before. The MA part sets the first step; the AR part sets the decay after it. That is the true model of this seed.

screens.title: ARMA(1, 1)
screens.prose: The model you just tuned is an **ARMA(1, 1)**: one autoregressive term and one moving-average term, $$x_t = c + \phi x_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t + \theta\varepsilon_{t-1}.$$ After lag 1 the shock term is spent, so each lag is a fixed multiple of the one before.

let.r1: (1 + phi * theta) * (phi + theta) / (1 + 2 * phi * theta + theta * theta)

screens.question: With $\phi = 0.7$ and $\theta = 0.4$, what is $\rho_2 / \rho_1$?

hints.text: Read the caption: lag 2 over lag 1.
Compare the green bars at lags 1 and 2.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the lag-2 theory bar by the lag-1 bar.

byKey.theta: You used $\theta$. The MA term only reaches one lag; the decay from lag 1 on is the AR part.
byKey.prod: You multiplied $\phi\theta$. The ratio between later lags is $\phi$ alone.
byKey.sum: You added the two coefficients. A ratio above 1 would make the ACF grow.

explain.text: From lag 2 on, $\rho_k = \phi\rho_{k-1}$, as in an AR(1). The MA term only changes where the decay starts: $\rho_1 = 0.819$ instead of $0.7$. So the ACF tails off like an AR, and the PACF tails off like an MA.

screens.title: Scoring the candidates
screens.prose: We fit every ARMA($p$, $q$) with $p, q \le 2$ by maximum likelihood and score each with $$\text{AIC} = 2k - 2\ell,$$ where $\ell$ is the maximised log-likelihood and $k$ counts every estimated parameter: the constant, the $\phi$s, the $\theta$s and $\sigma^2$.
screens.question: Fill in the two missing AICs, to 2 places.

hints.text: $2k - 2\ell$, and $\ell$ is negative.
ARMA(1, 1) has $k = 4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $2k - 2\ell$ with $k = 4$ and $k = 6$.

byKey.r1c2: Check the ARMA(1, 1) cell: $2 \times 4 - 2 \times (-710.224)$. Count $\sigma^2$ and the constant in $k$.

explain.text: ARMA(1, 1): $8 + 1420.448 = 1428.45$. ARMA(2, 2) has a slightly higher $\ell$, but two more parameters cost 4 points, so its AIC is 1430.61. The penalty $2k$ charges each parameter for the fit it buys.

screens.title: Within two points
screens.prose: A rule of thumb: AIC differences below 2 do not separate two models. Here is the whole grid for seed 33. These values agree between desktop statsmodels and the one in your browser.
screens.question: Tap every model within 2 of the smallest AIC, the smallest included.

hints.text: Find the smallest number first.
The smallest is ARMA(1, 1), 1428.45.
Anything up to 1430.45 counts: 1429.20 and 1429.55 do, 1430.61 does not.

feedback.correct: Correct. Three models tie; we keep the smallest, ARMA(1, 1).
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the models with AIC at most 1430.45.

byKey.with22: ARMA(2, 2) is 1430.61, which is 2.16 above the best: just outside the tie.
byKey.r2c1: ARMA(2, 0) is 1433.57, more than 5 points worse.

explain.text: ARMA(1, 2) and ARMA(2, 1) sit within 1.1 of ARMA(1, 1), so the data cannot tell them apart. Parsimony breaks the tie: take the model with fewest parameters, ARMA(1, 1). It is also the true model.

screens.prose: `ARIMA(x, order=(p, 0, q)).fit()` fits an ARMA($p$, $q$) with a constant (the 0 in the middle means no differencing). The fitted result has `.aic`, `.bic`, `.llf` and `.params`. Each fit takes about half a second here.

screens.title: A heavier penalty
screens.prose: The **BIC** charges $\ln n$ per parameter instead of 2: $$\text{BIC} = k\ln n - 2\ell.$$ With $n = 500$, $\ln n = 6.215$, so each parameter costs about three times as much. Here is the ARMA(1, 1) fit.
screens.question: What is the BIC of the ARMA(1, 1), to 2 places?

hints.text: Count $k$ from the table, leaving out the log-likelihood row.
Four parameters: rows 1 to 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $k = 4$, the natural log of 500, and $-2\ell$.

byKey.aic: That is the AIC, with 2 per parameter. The BIC uses $\ln 500 \approx 6.215$ per parameter.
byKey.k3: You left out $\sigma^2$. It is estimated too, so $k = 4$.
byKey.log10: You used $\log_{10}$. BIC uses the natural log.

explain.text: BIC 1445.31 is the lowest in the grid too, so both criteria agree here. The estimates sit near the truth: 0.7354 for 0.7 and 0.3866 for 0.4. Its residuals pass Ljung-Box with 2 degrees of freedom used up, `acorr_ljungbox(res.resid, lags=[10], model_df=2)` giving Q = 3.6617, p = 0.8863; a QQ plot of them is the next check, met in the `garch` course.

screens.title: Scored on the data that chose it
screens.prose: We fit both models on the first 400 days of seed 32 and keep the last 100 untouched. On the training days ARMA(2, 2) wins on AIC and on one-step error. Next we forecast each of the last 100 days one step ahead with the trained parameters.
screens.question: Which model will have the lower one-step MSE on the last 100 days?

options.text: ARMA(2, 2): it is better on both training scores
options.why: You trusted the training scores. They were measured on the days the parameters were fitted to.

options.why: Different parameters give different forecasts, so the errors differ.

The last column is empty for a reason.

feedback.correct: Correct. Out of sample ARMA(1, 1) scores 1.1122 against 1.1244.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Training scores reward fitting the noise in those 400 days.

byKey.22: You trusted the training scores. ARMA(2, 2)'s in-sample edge, 0.9126 to 0.8845, reverses on new days: 1.1122 to 1.1244.

explain.text: In sample ARMA(2, 2) led by 0.0281; out of sample it trails by 0.0122. Choosing a model by AIC and then quoting its error on the same data double-counts the fit, the same lie as training error in `stat-learning`. The honest comparison scores each model on days it never saw.

screens.title: An honest score
screens.prose: `res.apply(x)` runs the trained model over the whole series without refitting: its `fittedvalues` are one-step forecasts, each using only the days before it. As in the walk-forward lesson of `validation`, the test days never touch the parameters.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from statsmodels.tsa.arima.model import ARIMA

def oos_mse(x, order, n_train):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    res = ARIMA(x[:n_train], order=order).fit()      # parameters from training days only
    pred = res.apply(x).fittedvalues[n_train:]       # one-step forecasts, no refit
    return round(float(np.mean((x[n_train:] - pred) ** 2)), 3)

screens.title: ARMA($p$, $q$)
screens.prose: The general model has $p$ AR terms and $q$ MA terms: $$x_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^{p}\phi_i x_{t-i} + \varepsilon_t + \sum_{j=1}^{q}\theta_j\varepsilon_{t-j}.$$ Choose the orders with $\text{AIC} = 2k - 2\ell$ or $\text{BIC} = k\ln n - 2\ell$, break ties towards fewer parameters, then check residuals and out-of-sample error.
screens.question: How many parameters $k$ does an ARMA(2, 1) with a constant have?

options.why: You counted the $\phi$s and $\theta$ only. The constant and $\sigma^2$ are estimated too.
You left out one of the constant or $\sigma^2$. Both count.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count every number the fit estimates.

explain.text: $k = p + q + 2$ with a constant: here $2 + 1 + 2 = 5$, as statsmodels counts it.

screens.title: The interview question
screens.prose: An interviewer: "Your ARMA(4, 3) has the best AIC on two years of daily log volume for a FTSE stock. Would you put it into the desk's execution model?"
screens.question: Which answer is strongest?

options.text: Not yet: check smaller models within 2 AIC, the residuals with Ljung-Box, and the out-of-sample error; take the smallest model that passes
Yes: the best AIC already includes a penalty for its 9 parameters
options.why: You treated the AIC penalty as the whole check. AIC is measured in sample; with 9 parameters it can still fit noise, as seed 32 showed.

options.text: No: switch to BIC and use whatever it picks
options.why: You swapped one in-sample score for another. BIC is a useful second opinion, but neither replaces out-of-sample error.

hints.text: What has the AIC not been tested on?
Think of the three checks in this lesson.
Parsimony, residuals, out-of-sample error.

feedback.correct: Correct. That is the full modelling cycle.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. An in-sample score is where checking starts, not where it ends.

explain.text: Log volume is a good ARMA candidate: it is stationary and persistent within the day. But an ARMA(4, 3) has 9 parameters with the constant and $\sigma^2$, and AR and MA roots can nearly cancel. Prefer the smallest model whose residuals are white and whose walk-forward error is no worse.

ideas: When neither the ACF nor the PACF cuts off, the series needs both parts: ARMA($p$, $q$).
Fit a small grid and score it with AIC $= 2k - 2\ell$ or BIC $= k\ln n - 2\ell$; models within 2 AIC tie, so take the smallest.
Check the winner: white residuals by Ljung-Box, and one-step error on days the fit never saw.

formula.name: ARMA($p$, $q$)
formula.note: $k = p + q + 2$ with a constant and $\sigma^2$.

summary.trap: Choosing by AIC and quoting the error on the same days flatters the bigger model; score it out of sample.

quiz.prose: On the first 400 days of seed 32, an ARMA(5, 5) reaches $\ell = -540.82$, above ARMA(1, 1)'s $-549.82$.
quiz.question: What does the higher log-likelihood tell you?

options.text: Little: a bigger model never fits the training days worse

options.why: You read in-sample fit as forecasting skill. On the last 100 days ARMA(5, 5) scores 1.149 against 1.112.

options.text: It has found structure that ARMA(1, 1) missed
options.why: You read the gain as signal. The data are a true ARMA(1, 1); the 8 extra coefficients fit noise, and its AIC is only 2.0 lower.

feedback.correct: Correct. The likelihood can only rise as terms are added.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether extra terms can ever lower the training fit.

explain.text: Nested models: the ARMA(5, 5) can always set its extra terms to 0, so $\ell$ never falls. Its out-of-sample MSE is 1.149, the worst of the candidates.

options.text: White noise: the AR and MA parts cancel
An ARMA(1, 1) that the fit will recover as 0.5 and −0.5
options.why: You expected the fit to find the coefficients. They cancel, so any equal pair fits; statsmodels returns −0.1667 and 0.2265.
The MA term undoes the AR term exactly. Write both with the lag operator.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write both sides with the lag operator $L$.

explain.text: The common factor $(1 - 0.5L)$ cancels, leaving $x_t = \varepsilon_t$. AIC picks (0, 0) at 1376.23 against 1378.41 for (1, 1), whose fitted coefficients are unstable. When $\hat\phi \approx -\hat\theta$, drop both.
